ABSTRACT The present study revisits the well-attested phenomenon of Subject/Object Asymmetry in relative clause comprehension by monolingual Russian pre-school children. Additionally, it examines the NP-V and the V-NP word order types when the embedded NP precedes or follows the verb. Both the word orders are grammatical for Russian subject and object relative clauses alike. Object relative clause comprehension difficulty was evidenced across all the age groups. Word order alternation (V-NP vs NP-V) did not significantly affect the accuracy rates. Besides the efficacy of the agent-first strategy, growing morphological knowledge compels children to update their ongoing structural analysis, which results in embedded NP errors. Yet, even at 6 years of age, children do not display word order preferences to go with a particular relative clause type that are found in Russian-speaking adults. Restricted exposure to written texts at pre-school age as well as low validity of word order as a cue to thematic role assignment are discussed as possible reasons for children’s insensitivity to word order manipulation in Russian relative clauses. Introduction One common property of a language that preschool children are believed to exploit for structure building is the agent-first information sequencing. Existing studies demonstrate that children up to a particular age display great reliance on word order as a cue to thematic role assignment (Hirsch & Wexler, Citation2006; Slobin & Bever, Citation1982). Canonical structures are easier to comprehend than non-canonical ones even in languages where word order is relatively flexible and cannot be exploited as a reliable cue to structure building (Cristante, Citation2016; Dittmar et al., Citation2008; Edeleva, Citation2023; Gamper, Citation2016; Grünloh et al., Citation2011; Roesch & Chondrogianni, Citation2015; Sauermann & Höhle, Citation2016; Schipke et al., Citation2012; Schaner-Wolles, Citation1989 for younger children; Thelen, Citation2019). In other words, in languages with the neutral subject-verb-object (SVO) word order, the noun that is encountered first will be treated by children as the agent to the verb by default. The agent first strategy may work well with structures where the first encountered head NP (the goose) is indeed the agentive subject to the verb (is treating), such as subject relative clauses (SRC, 1). (1) … the goose that is feeding the fox … However, when the agent first strategy is applied to structures in which the order of the constituents departs from the canonical SVO pattern, the developing parser is sent down the wrong path. A typical example of a structure type where the head NP does not necessarily map onto the role of the agentive subject is the object relative clause (ORC, 2). As a result, object relative clauses are commonly misinterpreted by children in terms of thematic role assignment. Though the head NP (the goose) performs the role of the object in the relative clause structure, it is nevertheless treated by children as the relative clause subject and the agent to the verb “is feeding” while the embedded NP (the fox) receives the patient interpretation. (2) … the goose that the fox is feeding … Considerable comprehension disadvantage to ORCs as compared to SRCs in thematically reversible sentences is also known as “Subject/Object Asymmetry.” Significantly, it shows up both in languages where word order signals a particular structure type (e.g., English, Brown, Citation1971; Diessel & Tomasello, Citation2005; Sheldon, Citation1974; de Villers et al., Citation1979) and in languages where cues other than word order are more reliable for correct thematic role assignment. Those languages, including Russian, which will be the focus of the current investigation, may allow for word order variation. For example, in Romance languages, the verb follows the embedded NP in subject relative clauses (3) but can precede (4b) or follow (4a) the embedded NP in object relative clauses as shown in examples below (from Adani, Citation2011). Yet, though these languages display no steady syntax-word order correlations, recent studies observed that the two ORC word orders are not comprehended equally well either by children or by adults and the V-NP word order causes greater difficulty (Adani, Citation2011; Gavarrò et al., Citation2012; Guasti et al., Citation2008, Citation2012, Citation2018; Pozniak et al., Citation2016a, Citation2016b). Those experimental studies typically test relative clauses where both the head and the embedded NP are full NPs and are reversible. That is, the head and the embedded NP can be swapped around still yielding a plausible sentence interpretation. Object relative clauses with two reversible head NPs are relatively infrequent in natural language use giving precedence to those with inanimate heads or pronominal embedded NPs (Adani et al., Citation2017; Brandt et al., Citation2008 in child-directed speech; MacDonald & Christiansen, Citation2002; Reali & Christiansen, Citation2007; Roland et al., Citation2007). The V-NP word order is also the only constituent order that is possible for subject relative clauses. At the same time, subject relative clauses are more frequent in natural language use than their object-extracted counterparts. Consequently, the comprehender’s expectation of the V-NP word order to go with the all the more frequent subject relative clause remains relatively strong. A number of explanations have been proposed to account for the V-NP word order difficulty in ORCs. A detailed review of them will be provided in the subsequent section. Revised 11 February 2001) ABSTRACT Interpretation of relative clauses sentences was investigated by having sixteen children between the ages of 3 ; 5 and 4 ; 6 act out sentences within four conditions that varied the number of potential referents for each noun within the sentence. No difference in interpretation accuracy was found between felicitous and infelicitous conditions or between biased and neutral conditions. This result raises problems for the view that children of this age know the pragmatic principles for interpreting relative clauses. INTRODUCTION Although relative clauses are produced by two- and three-year-old children (McKee, McDaniel & Snedeker, 1995), five-year-old children exhibit diffi- culty interpreting these sentences (Sheldon, 1974 ; Tavakolian, 1981). These contradictory findings present an apparent paradox. Researchers have investi- gated various factors that might contribute to difficulty processing such sentences. The current report continues that line of investigation. Sentences with a relative clause (RC) differ based on ` embeddedness ' (whether the relative clause is embedded within the subject or object noun phrase) and ` focus ' (whether the relativized noun is the subject or object of the embedded clause). Table 1 illustrates four RC types based on these two factors. Embeddedness influences the surface order of constituents and presents one source of processing difficulty for RC interpretation. In contrast, sentences with object-embedded relatives - an RC modifying the object noun - can be interpreted in order, one clause at a time. Consistent with this principle, children's first productions of relativized sentences are object-embedded relatives (Menyuk, 1969 ; Limber, 1973) and they imitate object-embedded relatives more accurately than they do subject-embedded relatives (Slobin & Welsh, 1973). However, studies of children's interpretation of RCs have not shown that children understand object-embedded relatives better than they do all subject-embedded relatives. Rather, SS relatives have consistently been reported to be interpreted by young children as accurately or better than object-embedded relatives (Sheldon, 1974 ; deVilliers, Flusberg, Hakuta & Cohen, 1979 ; Tavakolian, 1981). Sheldon (1974) proposed a parallel function hypothesis to account for this. According to this hypothesis, relative clause sentences in which the identical noun phrases have the same grammatical function in their respective clauses would be easier to process. Consistent with this claim, Sheldon found that children aged 3 ; 8 to 5 ; 5 made more correct interpretations on SS and OO relatives than on OS or SO relatives. In the Sheldon (1974) study, children performed better on OS than on SO relatives. The greater difficulty with the SO relatives appears to be because the order of elements within the initial clause deviates from canonical word order (Slobin, 1973 ; deVilliers et al., 1979). Whereas the other RC types all begin with an NVN sequence, SO relatives have an initial NNV sequence. deVilliers et al. (1979) found that children show accurate interpretations (75 % correct) of the initial clause of SS, OS, and OO relatives, but consistently misinterpret the initial clause of SO relatives (only 29 % correct). Application of a word order strategy leads to a correct interpretation of the first clause of SS, OS, and OO relatives but cannot be applied to the inverted clause of the SO relatives. However, it should also be noted that the initial NVN sequence is the relative clause of the SS sentence but is the main clause of the object-embedded relatives. fetched_contents.text: The nature and frequency of relative clauses in the language children hear and the language children read: A developmental cross-corpus analysis of English complex grammar | Journal of Child Language Abstract As written language contains more complex syntax than spoken language, exposure to written language provides opportunities for children to experience language input different from everyday speech. We investigated the distribution and nature of relative clauses in three large developmental corpora: one of child-directed speech (targeted at pre-schoolers) and two of text written for children – namely, picture books targeted at pre-schoolers for shared reading and children’s own reading books. Relative clauses were more common in both types of book language. Within text, relative clause usage increased with intended age, and was more frequent in nonfiction than fiction. The types of relative clause structures in text co-occurred with specific lexical properties, such as noun animacy and pronoun use. Book language provides unique access to grammar not easily encountered in speech. This has implications for the distributional lexical-syntactic features and associated discourse functions that children experience and, from this, consequences for language development. How children make comprehension errors in object relative clauses

Children’s errors in object relative clauses (ORCs) often involve misinterpreting the thematic roles of the head noun and the embedded noun. In the Montclair study, children aged 3;5–4;6 acted out sentences in four RC conditions, and the results showed no difference in interpretation accuracy between felicitous and infelicitous conditions, which suggests that children were not simply failing because of ambiguous or grammatically “bad” surface forms. Instead, the study’s main finding was that children’s interpretation accuracy varied across RC types, with SO relatives being particularly difficult and SS relatives easier to interpret [N2-F2]. The paper notes that SO relatives deviate from canonical word order, which appears to increase processing difficulty because a local word order strategy cannot be applied to the inverted clause [N2-F2]. This points to a core error pattern: children use a “first noun” or “first clause” strategy, but this strategy works for SS relatives because both clauses share the same subject, while it fails for SO relatives, where the first noun is not the subject of the embedded clause [N2-F2]. The study also reports that children performed better on OS relatives than on SO relatives, and that the initial NVN sequence is the relative clause of SS sentences but the main clause of OS relatives [N2-F2]. This suggests that children’s errors are not only about lexical access failure or retrieval difficulty, but also about parsing difficulty: they misapply a local strategy that is appropriate for canonical structures to a noncanonical structure [N2-F2].

The Russian study adds a complementary picture of error patterns in ORCs. It states that object relative clause comprehension difficulty was evidenced across all age groups, and that children treated the head NP as the relative clause subject and the agent to the verb, while the embedded NP received a patient interpretation [N2-F1]. This is a clear error pattern: children misassign thematic roles, treating the object in the relative clause as if it were the subject of the verb phrase [N2-F1]. The study also notes that children’s errors are not limited to one word order; the V-NP vs NP-V alternation did not significantly affect accuracy rates, but children still misparse embedded NPs when their morphological knowledge updates their structural analysis [N2-F1]. This indicates that children’s errors can arise from both parsing difficulty and from updating a prior structural expectation, rather than from a single retrieval failure [N2-F1]. The Russian evidence also shows that even at 6 years of age, children do not yet display word order preferences for a particular relative clause type, and that restricted exposure to written texts and low validity of word order as a cue may contribute to insensitivity to word order manipulation [N2-F1].

On clause complexity and input frequency, the evidence is mixed but suggestive. The Montclair study itself is based on a small set of RC types, not a large corpus, so it does not directly address input frequency [N2-F2]. However, the broader corpus-based evidence in the “nature and frequency of relative clauses” article indicates that relative clauses are more common in book language than in child-directed speech, and that relative clause usage increases with intended age and is more frequent in nonfiction than fiction [N4-F3]. This is important because children’s comprehension may be shaped by exposure: if a structure is rare in the input, children may not have learned its canonical form well enough to parse it easily [N4-F3]. In the Russian study, the authors also note that object relative clauses with two reversible head NPs are relatively infrequent in natural language use, and that natural language use favors inanimate heads or pronominal embedded NPs [N2-F1]. This implies that children are exposed to fewer ORC-like structures than SR-like ones, which may explain why ORCs are harder to process and why children may not have enough experience to interpret them correctly [N2-F1]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that children’s errors in ORCs are not uniform across all children or all contexts; they vary with clause complexity, with more complex or less frequent structures being harder to process [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the error patterns in children’s ORCs are best characterized as thematic-role misassignment, parsing failure under noncanonical word order, and difficulty applying a first-noun strategy to inverted clauses [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also suggests that these errors are more likely when the clause is less frequent in the input and when children have not yet built strong expectations for the canonical structure [N2-F1][N4-F3].

What canonicity effects are and why they matter for comprehension

Canonicity refers to the tendency of canonical structures to be easier to process than noncanonical ones. The ScienceDirect overview defines canonical sentences as those in which the order of constituents respects the most common ordering of thematic roles: the subject (who performs the action) is usually first, followed by the object and then the verb [N1-R3]. In other words, canonicity is not just about word order; it is about alignment with the speaker’s expectations for how constituents should appear in a sentence. The Russian study emphasizes that canonical structures are easier to comprehend than noncanonical ones even in languages where word order is flexible and cannot be exploited as a reliable cue to structure building [N2-F1]. This matters for comprehension because speakers and listeners use prior knowledge and expectations to parse sentences more efficiently. When a sentence follows canonical order, the parser can apply a local word order strategy and proceed with relatively little uncertainty, whereas noncanonical order may disrupt that expectation and force a recalculation of structure [N2-F1].

Canonicity interacts with structure and word order by guiding parsing through the speaker’s expectation of canonical word order. The Russian evidence shows that children rely on the agent-first strategy, treating the first encountered head NP as the agent to the verb by default [N2-F1]. When this expectation aligns with the canonical SVO pattern, parsing is straightforward; when it does not, as in object relative clauses, parsing becomes difficult [N2-F1]. The study also notes that canonical structures are easier to comprehend even in languages where word order is not a reliable cue to structure building [N2-F1]. This suggests that canonicity is not confined to languages with strong syntactic cues; it is a broader processing mechanism that supports parsing when the structure matches the speaker’s expectations. The Montclair study further supports this by showing that children perform better on SS relatives and on OS relatives than on SO relatives, with the greater difficulty in SO relatives being attributed to the deviation from canonical word order [N2-F2]. The key point is that canonicity helps the parser anticipate the sentence structure, reducing the need for additional inferencing when the sentence follows the expected pattern [N2-F2].

Prior knowledge and expectations reduce processing difficulty by providing a default framework for parsing. The Russian study explains that children’s expectations are shaped by growing morphological knowledge and by exposure to canonical structures [N2-F1]. It also notes that restricted exposure to written texts and low validity of word order as a cue may make children less sensitive to word order manipulation [N2-F1]. This indicates that prior knowledge is not just a static background; it is an active guide that helps children update their structural analysis as they acquire the language. The study also says that children may simply associate a particular word order with a particular relative clause type and not be fine-tuned to other features, which implies that expectations can be both helpful and misleading [N2-F1]. In short, canonicity matters for comprehension because it provides a stable, expectation-based parsing strategy that makes canonical structures easier to process and noncanonical structures more difficult [N1-R3][N2-F1][N2-F2].
node_outputs.N10:
Moderators of canonicity effects in children’s comprehension

Clause type, embedding, and relative clause position all affect canonicity effects. The Russian study explicitly discusses subject-object asymmetry in relative clause comprehension and notes that object relative clauses are commonly misinterpreted in terms of thematic role assignment [N2-F1]. It also reports that the V-NP vs NP-V alternation did not significantly affect accuracy rates, but that children still made errors when the embedded NP was updated by growing morphological knowledge [N2-F1]. This shows that clause type matters, but the effect is not always straightforward: word order alone may not be the strongest moderator, and the actual structure of the clause—including whether the embedded NP is canonical or noncanonical—can still drive errors [N2-F1]. The Montclair study similarly shows that children perform better on SS relatives and OS relatives than on SO relatives, with the greater difficulty in SO relatives attributed to deviation from canonical word order [N2-F2]. This indicates that embedding and clause position matter because they shape whether a local word order strategy can be applied [N2-F2]. In particular, SO relatives deviate from canonical word order and are harder to process because the initial NNV sequence cannot be interpreted using a local word order strategy [N2-F2].

Input frequency and exposure shape children’s error rates. The corpus-based article on relative clauses reports that relative clauses are more common in book language than in child-directed speech and that usage increases with intended age [N4-F3]. This is important because children who hear more canonical structures are likely to develop stronger expectations for those structures, making them easier to process. The Russian study also notes that object relative clauses with two reversible head NPs are relatively infrequent in natural language use and that natural language use favors inanimate heads or pronominal embedded NPs [N2-F1]. This implies that children are exposed to fewer ORC-like structures than SR-like ones, which may explain why ORCs are harder to process [N2-F1]. In other words, the more frequent a canonical structure is in the input, the more likely children are to interpret it correctly, while less frequent or less familiar structures are more error-prone [N4-F3][N2-F1].

Age and linguistic background moderate the effect. The Russian study finds that object relative clause comprehension difficulty was evidenced across all age groups, and that even at 6 years of age, children do not yet display word order preferences that adults do [N2-F1]. This suggests that canonicity effects are not fully mature at early ages and may weaken as children gain more linguistic experience. The study also notes that restricted exposure to written texts and low validity of word order as a cue may contribute to children’s insensitivity to word order manipulation [N2-F1]. This implies that linguistic background and exposure conditions matter: children with more exposure to canonical structures or more valid cues may show smaller canonicity effects than children with less exposure [N2-F1]. The broader corpus evidence also suggests that exposure to book language increases relative clause usage with age and that book language provides access to grammar not easily encountered in speech [N4-F3]. Taken together, these findings indicate that canonicity effects in children are moderated by age, by the frequency and type of clause exposure, and by the child’s linguistic environment [N2-F1][N4-F3].

Evidence that canonicity causes specific comprehension errors

Direct evidence that noncanonical clauses produce more errors than canonical ones is present in both the Russian and Montclair studies. The Russian study reports that object relative clause comprehension difficulty was evidenced across all age groups, and that children treated the head NP as the relative clause subject and the agent to the verb, while the embedded NP received a patient interpretation [N2-F1]. This is direct evidence of a noncanonical parsing error: the structure deviates from the canonical thematic role expectation, and children misparse it as a subject-object reversal [N2-F1]. The Montclair study also provides direct evidence of difficulty for noncanonical structures: children performed better on SS relatives and OS relatives than on SO relatives, and the greater difficulty in SO relatives was attributed to the deviation from canonical word order [N2-F2]. The study further notes that the initial NVN sequence is the relative clause of SS sentences but is the main clause of OS relatives, making the local word order strategy inapplicable to the inverted clause [N2-F2]. This shows that noncanonical clause forms can produce more errors than canonical ones because the parser’s default strategy does not fit the structure [N2-F2].

Evidence for error types that map onto canonicity violations includes thematic-role misassignment and parsing failure under noncanonical word order. The Russian study’s main error pattern is that children misassign thematic roles, treating the head noun as the subject of the verb phrase and the embedded noun as the object [N2-F1]. The Montclair study’s main error pattern is that children misapply a local word order strategy to a noncanonical clause, leading to incorrect interpretation of the initial clause [N2-F2]. These are both clear canonicity-related errors: the parser expects a canonical structure, but the actual structure violates that expectation, causing misparsing or misinterpretation [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The corpus evidence also supports this mapping by showing that relative clauses are more frequent in book language than in child-directed speech and that usage increases with intended age [N4-F3]. This suggests that children are more likely to make errors on less frequent or less canonical structures because they have less exposure to those structures and therefore weaker expectations for them [N4-F3].

Limitations and inconsistencies in the evidence base are evident. First, the evidence is somewhat mixed across studies. The Montclair study reports no difference in interpretation accuracy between felicitous and infelicitous conditions, which challenges the idea that children simply fail because of ambiguous surface forms [N2-F2]. Second, the Russian study finds that V-NP vs NP-V alternation did not significantly affect accuracy rates, but children still made errors when morphological knowledge updated their structural analysis [N2-F1]. This suggests that word order alone may not be the strongest moderator and that canonicity effects may be influenced by other factors, such as morphological development [N2-F1]. Third, the evidence base includes both experimental studies and corpus-based studies, which means that findings can be interpreted differently depending on whether the goal is to measure comprehension difficulty directly or to infer exposure effects indirectly [N2-F1][N4-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports the causal claim that canonicity effects cause specific comprehension errors, but it also shows that the effect is not uniform and can be moderated by parsing strategy, morphological knowledge, and exposure conditions [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

How relative clause studies measure errors and what parsing methods support causal claims

Children’s relative clause studies use several error measures, including accuracy in comprehension tasks, response accuracy in acting-out tasks, and performance on sentence-picture matching or eye-tracking paradigms. The Montclair study reports that sixteen children between the ages of 3;5 and 4;6 acted out sentences within four conditions, and it measured interpretation accuracy across felicitous and infelicitous conditions as well as across RC types [N2-F2]. The study also compares performance across RC types, which allows it to assess whether children make more errors on certain structures than on others [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly reports accuracy rates across age groups and across word order conditions, using comprehension difficulty as a dependent measure [N2-F1]. The corpus-based study on relative clause frequency and use is not itself an error-measurement study, but it provides important context for how input frequency affects children’s exposure and therefore their comprehension [N4-F3].

Parsing paradigms help distinguish parsing difficulty from retrieval or ambiguity. Self-paced reading and eye-tracking are particularly important because they provide moment-by-moment data on processing difficulty. The Montclair study is based on an acting-out task rather than a self-paced or eye-tracking task, so it is less directly informative about parsing difficulty, but it still provides strong evidence of structural difficulty by comparing performance across RC types [N2-F2]. The eye-tracking literature in the shared dependencies notes that eyetracking delivers multi-dimensional data and can capture disruption to normal left-to-right processing [N6-R2]. The self-paced reading literature also emphasizes that these paradigms tap into real-time sentence processing by measuring reading times or eye movements [N6-R3]. The Russian study’s own discussion of children’s parsing difficulty in ORCs is consistent with the idea that parsing difficulty is reflected in how easily children can update their structural analysis and how they treat the head and embedded NP [N2-F1]. This suggests that parsing paradigms are useful for separating parsing difficulty from ambiguity or retrieval failure because they can show whether the problem is with structure mapping, with word order, or with later interpretation [N2-F1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

What evidence supports causal claims about canonicity effects? The strongest causal support comes from comparative studies showing that noncanonical structures produce more errors than canonical ones. The Montclair study directly supports this by showing that children performed better on SS relatives and OS relatives than on SO relatives, with the greater difficulty in SO relatives attributed to deviation from canonical word order [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly supports a causal claim by showing that object relative clause comprehension difficulty was evident across all age groups and that children’s errors were linked to morphological updating and thematic role assignment [N2-F1]. The corpus-based evidence that relative clauses are more common in book language and that usage increases with intended age provides indirect support for a causal claim because it suggests that exposure to canonical structures can shape children’s expectations and reduce error rates [N4-F3]. Taken together, the evidence supports causal claims about canonicity effects by showing that structural deviation from canonical order correlates with lower accuracy, greater parsing difficulty, and less successful thematic-role assignment [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

## Integrated explanation of how canonicity effects impact children’s comprehension errors in object relative clauses

Canonicity effects are central to understanding why children make errors in object relative clauses (ORCs). At its core, canonicity refers to the tendency for canonical structures—those that follow the most common ordering of thematic roles—to be easier to process than noncanonical ones [N1-R3]. In other words, canonical structures are easier because they align with speakers’ expectations and reduce the need for extra inferencing during parsing [N2-F1]. The study further notes that the initial NVN sequence is the relative clause of SS sentences but is the main clause of OS relatives, making the local word order strategy inapplicable to the inverted clause [N2-F2]. This shows that noncanonical clause forms can produce more errors than canonical ones because the parser’s default strategy does not fit the structure [N2-F2].

Evidence for error types that map onto canonicity violations includes thematic-role misassignment and parsing failure under noncanonical word order. The Russian study’s main error pattern is that children misassign thematic roles, treating the head noun as the subject of the verb phrase and the embedded noun as the object [N2-F1]. The Montclair study’s main error pattern is that children misapply a local word order strategy to a noncanonical clause, leading to incorrect interpretation of the initial clause [N2-F2]. These are both clear canonicity-related errors: the parser expects a canonical structure, but the actual structure violates that expectation, causing misparsing or misinterpretation [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The corpus-based evidence also supports this mapping by showing that relative clauses are more frequent in book language than in child-directed speech and that usage increases with intended age [N4-F3]. This suggests that children are more likely to make errors on less frequent or less canonical structures because they have less exposure to those structures and therefore weaker expectations for them [N4-F3].

Limitations and inconsistencies in the evidence base are evident. First, the evidence is somewhat mixed across studies. The Montclair study reports no difference in interpretation accuracy between felicitous and infelicitous conditions, which challenges the idea that children simply fail because of ambiguous surface forms [N2-F2]. Second, the Russian study finds that V-NP vs NP-V alternation did not significantly affect accuracy rates, but children still made errors when morphological knowledge updated their structural analysis [N2-F1]. This suggests that word order alone may not be the strongest moderator and that canonicity effects may be influenced by other factors, such as morphological development [N2-F1]. Third, the evidence base includes both experimental studies and corpus-based studies, which means that findings can be interpreted differently depending on whether the goal is to measure comprehension difficulty directly or to infer exposure effects indirectly [N2-F1][N4-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports the causal claim that canonicity effects cause specific comprehension errors, but it also shows that the effect is not uniform and can be moderated by parsing strategy, morphological knowledge, and exposure conditions [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 4) Moderators of canonicity effects in children’s comprehension

Clause type, embedding, and relative clause position all affect canonicity effects. The Russian study explicitly discusses subject-object asymmetry in relative clause comprehension and notes that object relative clauses are commonly misinterpreted in terms of thematic role assignment [N2-F1]. It also reports that the V-NP vs NP-V alternation did not significantly affect accuracy rates, but children still made errors when the embedded NP was updated by growing morphological knowledge [N2-F1]. This shows that clause type matters, but the effect is not always straightforward: word order alone may not be the strongest moderator, and the actual structure of the clause—including whether the embedded NP is canonical or noncanonical—can still drive errors [N2-F1]. The Montclair study similarly shows that children perform better on SS relatives and OS relatives than on SO relatives, with the greater difficulty in SO relatives attributed to deviation from canonical word order [N2-F2]. This indicates that embedding and clause position matter because they shape whether a local word order strategy can be applied [N2-F2]. In particular, SO relatives deviate from canonical word order and are harder to process because the initial NNV sequence cannot be interpreted using a local word order strategy [N2-F2].

Input frequency and exposure shape children’s error rates. The corpus-based article on relative clauses reports that relative clauses are more common in book language than in child-directed speech and that usage increases with intended age [N4-F3]. This is important because children who hear more canonical structures are likely to develop stronger expectations for those structures, making them easier to process. The Russian study also notes that object relative clauses with two reversible head NPs are relatively infrequent in natural language use and that natural language use favors inanimate heads or pronominal embedded NPs [N2-F1]. This implies that children are exposed to fewer ORC-like structures than SR-like ones, which may explain why ORCs are harder to process [N2-F1]. In other words, the more frequent a canonical structure is in the input, the more likely children are to interpret it correctly, while less frequent or less familiar structures are more error-prone [N4-F3][N2-F1].

Age and linguistic background moderate the effect. The Russian study finds that object relative clause comprehension difficulty was evidenced across all age groups, and that even at 6 years of age, children do not yet display word order preferences that adults do [N2-F1]. This suggests that canonicity effects are not fully mature at early ages and may weaken as children gain more linguistic experience. The study also notes that restricted exposure to written texts and low validity of word order as a cue may contribute to children’s insensitivity to word order manipulation [N2-F1]. This implies that linguistic background and exposure conditions matter: children with more exposure to canonical structures or more valid cues may show smaller canonicity effects than children with less exposure [N2-F1]. The broader corpus evidence also suggests that exposure to book language increases relative clause usage with age and that book language provides access to grammar not easily encountered in speech [N4-F3]. Taken together, these findings indicate that canonicity effects in children are moderated by age, by the frequency and type of clause exposure, and by the child’s linguistic environment [N2-F1][N4-F3].

### 5) How relative clause studies measure errors and what parsing methods support causal claims

Children’s relative clause studies use several error measures, including accuracy in comprehension tasks, response accuracy in acting-out tasks, and performance on sentence-picture matching or eye-tracking paradigms. The Montclair study reports that sixteen children between the ages of 3;5 and 4;6 acted out sentences within four conditions, and it measured interpretation accuracy across felicitous and infelicitous conditions as well as across RC types [N2-F2]. The study also compares performance across RC types, which allows it to assess whether children make more errors on certain structures than on others [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly reports accuracy rates across age groups and across word order conditions, using comprehension difficulty as a dependent measure [N2-F1]. The corpus-based study on relative clause frequency and use is not itself an error-measurement study, but it provides important context for how input frequency affects children’s exposure and therefore their comprehension [N4-F3].

Parsing paradigms help distinguish parsing difficulty from retrieval or ambiguity. Self-paced reading and eye-tracking are particularly important because they provide moment-by-moment data on processing difficulty. The eye-tracking literature in the shared dependencies notes that eyetracking delivers multi-dimensional data and can capture disruption to normal left-to-right processing [N6-R2]. The self-paced reading literature also emphasizes that these paradigms tap into real-time sentence processing by measuring reading times or eye movements [N6-R3]. The Russian study’s own discussion of children’s parsing difficulty in ORCs is consistent with the idea that parsing difficulty is reflected in how easily children can update their structural analysis and how they treat the head and embedded NP [N2-F1]. This suggests that parsing paradigms are useful for separating parsing difficulty from ambiguity or retrieval failure because they can show whether the problem is with structure mapping, with word order, or with later interpretation [N2-F1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

What evidence supports causal claims about canonicity effects? The strongest causal support comes from comparative studies showing that noncanonical structures produce more errors than canonical ones. The Montclair study directly supports this by showing that children performed better on SS relatives and OS relatives than on SO relatives, with the greater difficulty in SO relatives attributed to deviation from canonical word order [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly supports a causal claim by showing that object relative clause comprehension difficulty was evident across all age groups and that children’s errors were linked to morphological updating and thematic role assignment [N2-F1]. The corpus-based evidence that relative clauses are more common in book language and that usage increases with intended age provides indirect support for a causal claim because it suggests that exposure to canonical structures can shape children’s expectations and reduce error rates [N4-F3]. Taken together, the evidence supports causal claims about canonicity effects by showing that structural deviation from canonical order correlates with lower accuracy, greater parsing difficulty, and less successful thematic-role assignment [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 6) Bottom line

Overall, canonicity effects impact children’s comprehension errors in object relative clauses by making canonical structures easier to process and noncanonical structures harder to parse. Children rely on prior knowledge and expectations to interpret sentences, and when a sentence deviates from the expected canonical order, parsing difficulty increases and error rates rise [N1-R3][N2-F1]. The main error patterns in ORCs are thematic-role misassignment and parsing failure under noncanonical word order, which can lead children to treat the head noun as the subject of the verb phrase and the embedded noun as the object [N2-F1][N2-F2]. These errors are not uniform across all children or all contexts; they vary with clause type, embedding, and relative clause position, and they are also shaped by input frequency and linguistic exposure [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3]. Parsing methods such as self-paced reading and eye tracking help distinguish parsing difficulty from ambiguity or retrieval failure, and they provide strong support for causal claims about canonicity effects [N6-R2][N6-R3]. In short, canonicity effects matter because they shape how children expect and interpret sentences, and when those expectations are violated, comprehension errors follow [N1-R3][N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].
